analysis.one_liner: Requires veterinarians to give pet owners prescriptions so they can buy pet drugs elsewhere.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote in the Senate and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: Many pet medications require a prescription, and veterinarians are not always required to hand a written prescription to the owner — which makes it hard to comparison-shop at online or retail pharmacies that often sell the same drug for less. The bill would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to write rules requiring vets to give pet owners a copy of any prescription, send or verify it for a pharmacy on request, and forbidding vets from charging extra fees, requiring a purchase, or making owners sign liability waivers as the price of getting the prescription. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Pet owners who want to fill prescriptions at online or retail pharmacies instead of buying directly from the vet's office. These pharmacies commonly sell the same FDA-approved medications at lower prices, so owners with recurring prescriptions (flea, tick, heartworm, chronic conditions) would have saved money over time. Competitive pharmacies, including online pet pharmacies, would have gained a larger customer base.

how_it_helps.text: Veterinarians would have been required to give pet owners a copy of every prescription — before offering to fill it themselves — so owners could shop for the best price elsewhere [S3].

Vets could not condition the prescription on buying the drug from the practice, paying an extra fee beyond the exam, or signing a waiver of liability, which are the main levers used to keep fill revenue in-house [S3].
On request, vets would have had to transmit the prescription to a pharmacy and verify it, removing the practical friction that stops price comparison [S3].
Violations would have been enforceable by the FTC as unfair or deceptive practices, giving the rule real teeth [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Veterinary practices, which currently earn substantial revenue on prescription fills and refill cycles; the bill would have forced them to compete with online and retail pharmacies on price for the medications they prescribe.

drawbacks.text: Veterinary practices argue that prescription revenue helps keep exam fees lower, so shifting fills to outside pharmacies could mean higher upfront vet visit costs for all clients, including those who buy from the practice anyway.
The bill bars vets from disclaiming liability for accuracy of prescriptions provided to outside pharmacies, which could raise malpractice exposure concerns for prescribers [S3].
It adds FTC rulemaking and enforcement obligations for small veterinary businesses, a compliance cost that falls hardest on solo and small-animal practices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is recurring, direct savings for households with pets on long-term medications, and it mirrors rules that already apply to human doctors. The main honest cost is that veterinary clinics lose a profitable revenue stream and may adjust their pricing elsewhere. On balance the bill targeted a clear consumer bottleneck, though it died too early for those trade-offs to be litigated publicly.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee never took it up, so it never reached the Senate floor, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. Blumenthal introduced the Fairness to Pet Owners Act on July 31, 2014, with Democratic Sen. Schumer and Republican Sen. Lee as original cosponsors [S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
No further action was taken in the committee and no vote ever occurred; the bill died at the end of the 113th Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Veterinary practices that dispense their own prescriptions are better off, since nothing changed and they keep the prescription fill revenue that the bill would have exposed to pharmacy competition. Pet owners continue paying whatever their vet's office charges without a guaranteed right to shop elsewhere.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to the Commerce Committee, where it went no further.

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, making it bipartisan from day one.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 31, 2014 and never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from introduction — a Democrat (Blumenthal) sponsoring with one Democratic and one Republican cosponsor — and its death was procedural inaction, not a partisan floor vote; no roll calls occurred.

industries.note: Vet practices earn meaningful revenue dispensing prescriptions and refills at their own counters. The bill would have forced them to hand owners the prescription and compete with cheaper pharmacies, a direct hit to that revenue — their interest ran against owners' ability to comparison-shop.
Pharmacies would have gained access to prescriptions now locked inside vet practices, and their lower prices are exactly the savings owners stood to capture.
The bill did not change drug prices set by manufacturers, but wider pharmacy competition could compress dispensing margins and affect distribution channels between makers, vets, and pharmacies.
